title: Set a probe positioner on a probe station: slide it to the die, hold it as its magnet locks, trim its tip by knob
instruction: Set the loose probe positioner up on the marked die. Its magnet is off. Slide it along the platen until its needle points at the die with the tip near the mark, never touching the other needle, the wafer or the microscope. Keep it from shifting while you push its magnet lever to ON. Then turn its X and Y knobs to bring the tip over the mark, short of the other probe's tip. Let go.
context: Probing a chip on a manual wafer probe station starts by setting each probe positioner round the die. It stands on the steel platen on a switchable magnet: with the lever off it is slid until its needle is over the die, the lever is thrown to clamp it (MPI TS150 manual: 'The side "ON", "OFF" lever is used to toggle the magnetic clamping'), and the tip is then brought to its place with the positioner's micrometer knobs, tips '2-3 mm apart' before landing (MIT MTL IV-probe SOP). The positioner is the size of an MPI MP40: 65 x 40 mm base, 13 mm travel. Its tip is 14.4 cm from the base's centre, so a degree of twist moves it 2.5 mm; throwing the lever drags a free base unless it is held; each knob turn moves the tip 0.3 mm, with the other needle 2 mm beyond the mark. The task stops before the tips are lowered onto the pads.
setup: Positions in cm from the midpoint between the arm bases: x forward, y left; heights above the bench top. (1) Platen: nickel-plated steel 33.2 cm along x by 23.5 cm along y, 1.2 cm thick, its top 12 cm up, centred at (42, 0), with a 25 cm round opening over the chuck (MPI TS150 datasheet: about 330 x 235 mm, R125 opening), so steel remains at its near end (x 25.4 to 29.5 on the centre line, wider at the corners) and far end. Chuck 16 cm across, its top 28 mm below the platen top (datasheet minimum), with a 150 mm wafer 0.7 mm thick; the die is marked at its centre (42, 0) with a 1 mm cross. Microscope: a bridge across y at x 42 on posts at y +/-20, its lens (4.4 cm across) 4 cm above the wafer. (2) Positioner 1 is clamped on the far end, its base centred at (56.6, 0), needle pointing -x, tip 2 mm past the mark at (42.2, 0), 1 mm above the wafer. (3) Positioner 2 stands loose on the near end at (27.6, 6.5), lever OFF, needle pointing +x, tip 1 mm above the wafer at (42, 6.5), its X and Y stages centred. Both are MP40-class: base 65 mm along y by 40 mm along x (listing: 65 x 40 mm, 13 mm XYZ travel, magnetic mount), 100 mm tall, 0.6 kg; arm and 0.51 mm tungsten needle (0.020 in tip stock) reach 14.4 cm forward of the base's centre, the arm 4 cm above the platen and the needle sloping down to the tip (sizes, mass: estimates). Base on platen: friction 0.3 with the lever OFF (estimate); at ON the magnet pulls it down with 40 N (estimate; the maker gives no figure). Magnet lever on the base's +y face: a 3 cm arm hinged 4.5 cm up, standing up at OFF, with a flat 8 x 20 x 16 mm knob 14 mm off the face; it swings forward 70 degrees to its stop and counts as ON past 62 degrees; 3 N at the knob (estimate). X knob on the base's rear (-x) face, Y knob on its -y face: each a 16 mm cylinder standing 12 mm out, its axis 6 cm above the platen, 0.3 mm of tip travel per turn (MP40 screw resolution 300 um; estimate), 0.02 N m drag (estimate). Both YAM arms start at their ready pose, grippers open. Real trial: one manual positioner (a used MP40 or Signatone S-725 class unit, about USD 300 to 500, estimate) on a steel plate with the R125 opening, a printed wafer mark, a second fixed needle and a post at the lens height; read with a USB microscope camera and a printed scale; a continuity tester on each needle against a foil wafer stand-in flags a needle touch; a phone camera at the side and a phone level app read the tilt; the base's drift since the latch is read with a dial indicator against the base, and the tip's shift across the throw with the microscope reticle read before and after the throw; spare tungsten needles for a bent tip.
scoring: Read at the end the way a technician reads it: the tip against the mark on the station's microscope camera, through its reticle or scale bar (a person can read 0.3 mm there). 0.25: positioner 2 upright (tilt under 2 degrees), its needle within 5 degrees of the line to the mark, the tip within 4 mm of the mark in plan. 0.5: and the lever ON with the tip within 4 mm of the mark at the latch, the tip moved under 0.5 mm across the throw. 0.75: and the tip within 0.3 mm of the mark after the knobs were turned at least 90 degrees in all since the latch, the base moved under 0.5 mm since the latch. 1.0: and every fingertip 3 cm from positioner 2 and its needle, all still for 1 s, positioner 1 moved under 1 mm. 0: a needle touches the other needle, the wafer or the lens, or a fingertip touches a needle, the wafer or the lens.
reset_notes: Nothing is random: positioner 2 at its mark, lever OFF, knobs at zero. Check each needle for a bent tip before a trial.
fidelity: Rigid bodies, 240 Hz, GPU. Positioner 2's base is a free body on the platen (friction 0.3); its X and Y stages are sprung slides that code drives from each knob's angle (0.3 mm a turn); the magnet is a 40 N downward pull once the lever passes 62 degrees. Lever swing and force, knob drag, masses, needle reach: estimates. Needle collider 1.2 mm across (real 0.51 mm); needle contact scores on centre lines under 0.6 mm apart. The demo reads positioner 2's pose and joints, as the microscope would.
